data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible without induction by redefining rational action as the strategic selection of the most falsifiable (and thus most informative) survivor, accepting that this yields no probability of truth but maximizes the speed of error elimination.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the universe is fundamentally chaotic such that past survival implies no structural stability even for the purpose of error detection.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the scientist's goal shifts from truth-seeking to immediate practical reliability where inductive heuristics outperform critical selection.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'severity' of a test cannot be defined independently of background assumptions that themselves rely on induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism shifts the justification from 'likelihood of future success' (inductive) to 'severity of past testing' (deductive). A theory that has survived severe tests has exposed itself to greater risk of falsification; preferring it is rational not because it is likely true, but because it has withstood the strongest attempts to prove it false, making it the best available target for further criticism. This aligns with the goal of verisimilitude (truth-likeness) without assigning probabilities.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
